refuter_findings.location: Definition, paragraph beginning “Constraint set and admissible data”
refuter_findings.evidence: The definition calls M “symmetric positive definite” but cites [[def-invertible-matrix-and-general-linear-group]], which defines only a two-sided matrix inverse: “A matrix A … is invertible when there is a matrix B … such that AB=I_n=BA.” It does not define the required conditions Mᵀ=M and uᵀMu>0 for every nonzero u.

The remark allows the pendulum constraint G(q)=|q|²−l² “on all of R² with G_q≠0 off the origin.” But G_q=2q vanishes at the origin, while this definition requires rank k at every point of O, not only on G=0. Thus O=R×R² is not regular under the stated definition.

refuter_findings.location: Frontmatter deps; Definition, paragraph “Sample Lagrangian and zero applied force”
refuter_findings.evidence: The paragraph says L₀ is a special case of the chart “as in [[def-cm-time-dependent-lagrangian-and-action]]” and imports the meanings of stationary, action, and Euler–Lagrange expression from it, but that supplier is absent from deps. The declared prerequisite closure therefore omits a load-bearing definition.

It calls δS the “one-sided derivative at ε=0” without specifying a side, although q+εη is admissible for all sufficiently small |ε| and the displayed derivative notation is ordinary two-sided differentiation. The definition does not say which derivative it names.

refuter_findings.location: Definition, paragraph “The augmented functional and the vakonomic law”
refuter_findings.evidence: The vakonomic condition uses a “directionally one-sided derivative” at s=0 but states no limiting side; it also writes d/ds|ₛ₌₀. The derivative convention is consequently unspecified.

The text says B_t+B_q·v is “the derivative of B along that family” q↦q+sξ(q), t↦t. At fixed t that variation gives B_q·ξ. B_t+B_q·v is instead the total derivative of B(t,q(t)) along a trajectory with v=q′.

M is assumed “symmetric positive definite,” but no dependency in this item’s closure defines that matrix condition. [[def-euclidean-inner-product]] defines the Euclidean inner product and norm, not positive definiteness of a matrix. State Mᵀ=M and uᵀMu>0 for every nonzero u, or cite an exact definition.

The remark says the n×n matrix DXᵀMDX is positive definite “on the image of DX.” In the Statement DX maps Rⁿ to Rᵐ, so its image is a subspace of Rᵐ, whereas DXᵀMDX acts on Rⁿ. The claim needs to identify the pulled-back form on Rⁿ or the restriction of M to im(DX).

F3 asserts that an injective endomorphism of Rᵏ is invertible. The cited [[thm-linear-kernel-image-and-injectivity]] proves only injective iff trivial kernel, and [[def-invertible-matrix-and-general-linear-group]] defines invertibility by a two-sided inverse. Step 1.4 uses trivial kernel of C to conclude C is invertible without a finite-dimensional injective-to-surjective result.

F4 states that injectivity is equivalent to invertibility for finite-dimensional endomorphisms, but the dependencies provide definitions of linear maps and invertibility plus a determinant criterion, not the finite-dimensional injective-to-surjective result. Step 1.2 relies on that implication after the kernel computation.

F4 asserts an iff between A invertible and Aᵀu=0⇒u=0. Its cited converse, “the transpose of an invertible matrix is invertible,” proves A invertible⇒Aᵀ injective, not the reverse. Proof step 3.1 only needs that forward direction, so F4 overstates what is established.

Clause 4 first uses q:[a,b], but this statement has not bound a or b or specified a<b; unlike the cited Lagrangian-chart statements, it does not introduce a chart over [a,b]. The interval in the claim is therefore unbound.

F3 says “a linear map of Rⁿ with trivial kernel is bijective,” citing only invertibility and linear-map definitions. Step 1.2 uses this to invert G(t,q); no finite-dimensional injective-to-surjective result is supplied in the dependencies.

The proof writes L_q ∂qX and L_v ∂s∂qX. The cited gradient definition gives vectors in Rⁿ, while the Jacobian has output rows/input columns; under the column-gradient convention used by the related covariance item, these products have incompatible shapes. The chain rule and boundary term require transposed Jacobians.

F2 says the bump has “support in (t₁−ρ,t₁+ρ).” The scoped bump lemma states β>0 for |t−t₁|<ρ and β=0 for |t−t₁|≥ρ, so its topological support is the closed interval [t₁−ρ,t₁+ρ], including both endpoints. The closed interval still lies inside (a,b), but the stated support inclusion is false.

The step says “let y,z be the primitives” with the specified initial values, but neither constructs those functions nor cites a primitive-existence theorem; the item’s dependencies do not include the fundamental theorem needed for this use. For example, y(t)=arsinh(t) and z(t)=√(1+t²)−1 give the required derivatives.

The definition of d’Alembert motion allows any C² curve on an open interval satisfying the equations there. Restricting a motion to a smaller open interval containing 0 gives another motion with the same initial data, so the unqualified claim that “the d’Alembert motion is unique” is false; only the maximal solution, or uniqueness up to restriction, follows.

refuter_findings.location: Example clause 1; Facts F3 and Verification step 2.1
refuter_findings.evidence: The Statement gives the range of v/√(1+v²) as exactly (−1,1), but F3 and step 2.1 establish only containment in (−1,1) and that 1 is omitted. They do not show every p in (−1,1) is attained; solving v=p/√(1−p²) supplies the missing step.

The example concludes that q* is “not a local minimum” and refers to “nearby” admissible curves without specifying a topology or a variation-local convention on the C² curve space. The displayed family approaches q* in the C² topology, but that topology is not stated.

The derivative of K+U_g is evaluated at the phase point (π/4,1), then used to conclude it is not conserved along all solutions. No solution through that phase point is constructed or established in this step, so the pointwise derivative alone does not provide a solution witnessing nonconservation.

The remark says the theorem is stated “in that direction only,” but [[thm-cm-stationarity-iff-euler-lagrange]] states that stationarity holds if and only if E_L(q)=0. That theorem is an equivalence about stationarity, not a one-direction theorem about extrema; the separate extremum claim also does not specify a function-space notion of local extremum.

Step 2.1 concludes that M is bijective from a trivial kernel, but its dependencies contain no finite-dimensional rank-nullity result. In step 3.1, Sx=0⇒x=0 is used to conclude positive definiteness; the displayed identity xᵀSx=(M⁻¹ᐟ²x)ᵀK(M⁻¹ᐟ²x) should instead be applied to every nonzero x.

F4 attributes the Euclidean norm’s triangle and reverse-triangle inequalities to [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. That dependency explicitly says the norm property is proved separately in thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm and “is not assumed here.” Those inequalities are unused in the theorem’s proof, but the citation is inaccurate in the current carrier.

reader_findings.location: Facts F3, lines 87–89; Proof step 1.1, line 103
reader_findings.evidence: The argument infers bijectivity of G from a trivial kernel but cites only invertibility and linear-map definitions. Supply finite-dimensional injective-to-surjective reasoning, such as rank-nullity.

L_q and L_v are gradients in Rⁿ and ∂qX is a Jacobian with output rows/input columns, but the proof writes L_q∂qX and L_v∂qX with no compatible vector/matrix shape. The chain rule and boundary term require transposed Jacobians under the stated gradient convention.

The bump is positive inside (t₁−ρ,t₁+ρ) and zero outside the closed interval, so its topological support includes the endpoints and is not contained in that open interval. State the nonzero locus or the closed support interval.

y and z are introduced as primitives without construction or an existence theorem. The required FTC for continuous integrands is not in deps; define them by oriented integrals and cite FTC, or give explicit antiderivatives and verify their derivatives.

The explicit global curve is called the unique d'Alembert motion, but restrictions to different open intervals are also motions under the definition. State uniqueness of the maximal motion or uniqueness up to restriction.
The statement asserts range exactly (-1,1), but F3 establishes only containment and exclusion of p=1. Prove every p∈(-1,1) is attained, for example by solving v/√(1+v²)=p.

“Local minimum” and “nearby” require a topology or explicit variation-local convention on admissible curves, but none is specified. The decreasing one-parameter family gives a witness in the usual C² topology; state that topology or define the local comparison.

Strict-minimum and non-minimum claims require 1−cos θ>0 for small nonzero θ. Facts F1 gives only |cos θ|≤1, which is not strict. Include a local strictness argument, such as 1−cos θ=2sin²(θ/2) with local nonvanishing of sine.

A nonzero derivative formula at the phase point (π/4,1) does not by itself show that an actual solution passes through it. Apply local existence for the smooth phase vector field before using that point to show nonconservation.

The cited theorem is an equivalence between stationarity and the Euler–Lagrange equation, not a theorem stated only in the necessary-condition direction for extrema. Separate that equivalence from the first-order necessary condition for extrema and state its function-space notion.
The title uses p·ξ, but the item defines its charge using L_v and neither defines p nor depends on an exact p-definition. Replace p by L_v or bind p:=L_v.

Step 3.1 infers positive definiteness from a trivial kernel; the displayed quadratic-form identity should be applied to every nonzero x. Rank-nullity closes the first gap; a direct strict quadratic-form argument closes the second.
